title: The Lighthouse · 7
paragraphs: “Mrs. Ramsay!” Lily cried. “Mrs. Ramsay!” Nothing happened. The pain only grew. How anguish could reduce you to such a level of foolishness! she thought. At any rate the old man hadn’t heard her. He stayed kindly and calm—even sublime, if you wanted to see him that way. Thank heaven nobody had heard that humiliating cry of hers: stop, pain, stop! At least she hadn’t visibly lost her mind. Nobody had watched her step off her narrow strip of board into the waters of annihilation. She was still just a skimpy old maid on the lawn with a paintbrush in her hand.

And now, little by little, the pain of wanting, and the bitter anger (at being called back just when she believed she would never grieve for Mrs. Ramsay again—had she missed her among the coffee cups at breakfast? Not at all), grew less. What their anguish left behind, as a remedy, was a relief that soothed in itself, and also, more mysteriously, a sense that someone was there—Mrs. Ramsay, freed for a moment of the weight the world had laid on her, lingering lightly beside Lily and then (for this was Mrs. Ramsay in all her beauty) lifting to her forehead a wreath of white flowers and going off with it. Lily squeezed her tubes again and attacked the problem of the hedge. It was odd how clearly she could see Mrs. Ramsay stepping, quick as always, across fields that were soft and purplish in their folds, full of flowers—hyacinths or lilies—among which she vanished. It was a trick of the painter’s eye. For days after hearing of her death, Lily had seen her like this, raising the wreath to her forehead and going off unquestioningly across the fields with her companion, a shadow. The sight, and the phrase, had power to comfort. Wherever she was—painting here in the country, or in London—the vision would come, and her eyes would half close, searching for something to rest the vision on. She would look down the railway carriage, or the bus; take a line from someone’s shoulder or cheek; look at the windows across the way; at Piccadilly strung with lamps at evening. All of it had been part of the fields of death. But there was always something—a face, perhaps, or a voice, or a newsboy calling the evening papers, _Standard, News_—that pushed through, snubbed her, woke her, and demanded, and in the end received, an effort of attention, so that the vision had to be made again and again. Now once more, driven by some instinctive need for distance and for blue, she gazed down at the bay, turning the blue bars of the waves into little hills and the more purple patches into stony fields. And once again, as always, something that didn’t belong startled her. In the middle of the bay was a brown speck. It was a boat—she saw that after a second. But whose? Mr. Ramsay’s, she answered. Mr. Ramsay: the man who had marched past her, aloof, with his hand raised, leading a procession, in those beautiful boots of his, asking for sympathy she had refused to give. By now the boat was halfway across the bay.

Apart from a streak of wind here and there, the morning was so fine that sea and sky seemed woven from a single fabric, as though sails were fixed high in the sky, or clouds had fallen into the sea. Far out, a steamer had drawn a huge scroll of smoke across the air, and it hung there, curling and circling ornamentally, as though the air were a delicate gauze that held things gently in its mesh and only rocked them softly this way and that. And, as sometimes happens in very fine weather, the cliffs seemed aware of the ships and the ships aware of the cliffs, as if they were passing some secret signal of their own between them. For though it was sometimes so near the shore, this morning in the haze the Lighthouse seemed immensely far away.

“Where are they now?” Lily wondered, gazing out to sea. Where was he—that very old man who had walked past her without a word, with a brown paper parcel under his arm? The boat had reached the middle of the bay.
